facts.claim: Bleeding Verse is an AI-assisted project. Its YouTube and Instagram bios say it uses "AI-assisted instrumentation and vocals", so there is no human band lineup to credit.
Bleeding Verse's Spotify profile describes its process as human lyrics turned into songs with AI.
Shazam's credits for "Only When It's You" list Kyle Ward as songwriter, background vocalist and in production and engineering.
Deezer's credits for the track list Kyle Ward as writer and Bleeding Verse with Kyle Ward as composers.

"Only When It's You" is track 1 on The Anatomy of Hurt, a six-track release. It runs 4:14, and the track listing is followed by You Wanted Wanting, I Don't Ache Like I Used To, No Longer Yours To Haunt, Glass Chest and I Left The Light Off. Amazon dates the release 10 August 2025.
Apple Music files The Anatomy of Hurt as an EP and lists other versions of the song as separate releases: Only When It's You (Alternate) and Only When It's You (Acoustic).
An acoustic version of "Only When It's You" was released on September 26, 2025.

The lyrics, credited to Kyle Ward, are about feeling safe only with one person and being hurt only by that same person. They include the lines about being "the silence inside of the storm" and "static where you used to be".
Bleeding Verse's first album, I Became What You Broke, was uploaded to Spotify on July 25, 2025. It was followed by singles and The Anatomy of Hurt EP.

The project's YouTube bio says it is inspired by Dayseeker and Holding Absence. In late September 2025, Holding Absence frontman Lucas Woodland criticised the project after it passed his band's Spotify monthly listeners, and the project's creator replied on X that it was a "loving tribute".

research.lineage: The project describes itself as emotional post-hardcore and alt-rock/emo-leaning, modelled on Dayseeker and Holding Absence, with heartbreak-heavy melodies and cinematic soundscapes.

draft:
The chorus of **Only When It's You** hands one person two jobs at once. They are the only place the narrator feels safe, and the only thing that can actually hurt. Everything else (falling, breaking, losing) gets shrugged off in a single line, as if the rest of life doesn't register at all. That's the feeling the song holds: a love so total it has become the narrator's whole nervous system, and nobody in the song stops to ask whether that's healthy.

The best image is in the chorus. "You're the silence inside of the storm" turns the beloved into the calm eye. But the second verse quietly takes it back. The person who "pulled me free" is gone, and what's left is "static where you used to be." Silence was the gift; static is the loss. Across those two lines the narrator moves from shelter to interference without ever saying the word grief.

The bridge is where the song gets heavier than its hooks. "I was never whole when I was alone" arrives right after "If I disappear, let it be known," and the pairing is unsettling. It reads less like a romantic vow than like someone who has staked their sense of self on another person and is now watching it go. The last chorus adds "You're the ache I'll never show," a confession that the steadiness on the surface is a performance.

The writing isn't always this sharp. "Every thought just cuts like stone" is stock, and the second pre-chorus loses its rhyme, landing "less" against "brain" with a thud.

The sound is built for size. Distorted guitars hold sustained power chords in a thick wall, bass drives on the roots, and the snare hits hard over a steady mid-tempo beat. The lead voice is clean and mid-range, pushed into long, slightly strained notes, with a harmony stacked above it. The mix is polished, wide and dry. It's the emotional post-hardcore lineage the project names outright, Dayseeker and Holding Absence: big wounded choruses, lots of lift, little grit.

That lineage got pointed. Bleeding Verse describes itself as using "AI-assisted instrumentation and vocals" on human lyrics, with Kyle Ward credited as songwriter, background vocalist, producer and engineer. When it passed Holding Absence in Spotify monthly listeners, frontman Lucas Woodland criticised it, and the creator answered that it was a "loving tribute." The song opens the six-track *The Anatomy of Hurt*, and acoustic and alternate versions followed.

It sticks because it says the thing people in deep attachment rarely admit, that the person who makes you feel safe is the same one who can wreck you, and it makes you shout that along.
